a118.speaker: Catherine Bashiama, coffee farmer
a118.speech: Expresses gratitude to her community for the coffee she has planted, sharing her story of resilience after her husband’s accident left them struggling to afford their children’s education; with her coffee now blooming and bearing fruit, she looks forward to a more prosperous future.

a118.speaker: Seme Alfred, coffee farmer
a118.speech: “I’m thrilled to see my coffee maturing, and I’m finally starting to reap the financial rewards. I can truly sense the profits coming in.”

a118.speaker: Ian Paterson, managing director of Equatoria Teak
a118.speech: “During our experiments with various coffee types in South Sudan, a farmer pointed out that we have our own unique coffee here, known as Excelsa. This prompted us to conduct trials on it.” ; He believes that Excelsa is resilient to climate changes and presents significant opportunities for the coffee sector as environmental conditions evolve.

a118.speaker: Atoroba Peni, King of Azande
a118.speech: Appreciates local production and trade, emphasising its role in fostering self-sufficiency; highlights that a robust local industry reduces reliance on inconsistent government payments and foreign assistance, empowering the community ; emphasises the importance of self-reliance within the community, stating that reliance on external sources, such as government salaries or foreign aid, can lead to vulnerability — when salaries are delayed many struggle to meet their basic needs, and when aid is not received families face challenges in caring for their children — and advocates for individuals and communities to invest in coffee and other cash crops to foster independence and sustainability.

a197.speaker: Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC)
a197.speech: Has said more governors in the country will join the party ahead of the 2027 general election; speaking during the Bayelsa State chapter 12th expanded stakeholders meeting and endorsement for President Bola Tinubu, he stated that because President Tinubu has done well, more governors and Senators have abandoned their parties and joined APC to ensure that the president wins overwhelmingly in 2027, and that President Tinubu is on the move to take Nigeria to a greater height ; “Our doors are still open, more governors are still moving in to our party, more personalities are still moving in, senators, members of the House of representatives, because of the caliber, integrity and the output of the person we make president. Other people who are running around trying to challenge the president in the 2027 election, but of course you know, when you have a lion and other small animals are barking, the lion doesn’t even take notice of them, he goes about his duties properly, that is what the president is doing. It is expected that dogs will bark, it’s expected that opposition will speak and rise, but it is well assured that we have a product that even a blind man in this country will support overwhelmingly. I am very happy with the South South geopolitical zone, because all the governors that were in the other Political parties before have seen the quality of the character of the president... they have all abandoned their own political parties, and joined our great party... They are leaving their parties to come to APC to support Mr President in 2027 to record an overwhelming victory, so that as we go into 2027, governance will be easier. The President is not afraid; he takes the bull by the horn, what others do not have the political will to embark on, he goes about it and he achieves results, this president is on the move to take Nigeria to a greater height.” ; He called for the unity and togetherness of the party members in Bayelsa in order to record an overwhelming victory in the 2027 general election.

a197.speaker: Chief Timipre Sylva, former Governor of Bayelsa State
a197.speech: Stated that APC in Bayelsa State is very united ahead of the general election.

a266.speaker: Analysts
a266.speech: say the advance marks a turning point for the M23 since it launched a fresh insurgency into Congo's mineral-rich east in March 2022 ; say they never managed to gain this much ground during previous offensives in 2012 and 2013 and the more territory they take, the more opportunity there is for them to generate more mining revenue to fund their campaign ; say the group has spread into new territories in recent weeks where there is scope to generate more mining revenue

a266.speaker: M23 rebel group
a266.speech: accuses the government of not living up to the peace deal to fully integrate Congolese Tutsis into the army and administration.

a266.speaker: U.N. experts' report published this month
a266.speech: There are more than 8,000 M23 fighters, of which around 5,500 have been recruited since September, according to a U.N. experts' report published this month.

a266.speaker: United Nations
a266.speech: According to the U.N., M23 control of the coltan-mining region of Rubaya has allowed them to generate an estimated $800,000 per month through a production tax.

a266.speaker: Congo, Western powers and the United Nations
a266.speech: accuse neighbouring Rwanda of backing the group with its own troops and weapons.

a266.speaker: A local administrator and the head of a civil society group (anonymous)
a266.speech: said there were clashes with the army on Thursday morning [in Sake].

a266.speaker: Alice Maombi Tulinado, 28, a mother of four from Kalehe territory, displaced person
a266.speech: "We used to hear about the war from very far away," ; "We did not see the war coming upon us. Now it is in our homes," she said as she joined thousands of others already living in a makeshift camp there.

a266.speaker: Fred Bauma, head of a Congolese research group
a266.speech: "The capture of Minova isolates Goma a little more and opens the way to the capture of other localities ... important trade flows and mines."

a266.speaker: Congo's army
a266.speech: has so far only said that "the enemy has broken through" in Minova.

a266.speaker: Congolese national army spokesman
a266.speech: did not respond to requests for comment about the situation in Sake on Thursday.

a266.speaker: Jason Stearns, U.S.-based university professor and former U.N. expert
a266.speech: said Rwanda was probably not willing to risk a stronger international backlash and more aid cuts if the M23 tried to take Goma again and push further south into Bukavu, the capital of the adjacent South Kivu province ; said efforts by Angola to mediate a lasting ceasefire and de-escalate tensions between Congo and Rwanda were at an impasse ; "The next move has to be on the battlefield, which is why we have seen this escalation in recent weeks and the dramatic expansion of M23 territory."

a266.speaker: Athanase Zihalirwa Muderwa, Minova resident
a266.speech: "I am too hungry. The situation in Nzulo is not good either," ; "I don't know where I am going."

a375.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a375.speech: Stated on his social network: “They have ridiculously lost 400,000 soldiers, and many more civilians. There should be an immediate ceasefire and negotiations should begin.”

a375.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a375.speech: In an interview broadcast on Sunday, December 8 in the United States, warned that he fully intends to reduce American aid to Ukraine.

a375.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine
a375.speech: Has commented little on his meeting at the Elysee; warns about the complexity of the situation on his social networks.

a444.speaker: Marc Weinstock, U.S. Embassy Charge d'Affaires in Eswatini
a444.speech: Emphasized the United States' continued commitment to supporting Eswatini in addressing public health challenges: "PEPFAR and the U.S. Government remain committed to supporting countries in maintaining the response we have jointly built." ; "We look forward to continued collaboration under the United States' new Global Health Strategy that was released at UNGA last week. These vehicles that we hand over today represent resources provided by the United States."

a444.speaker: Khanyakwezwe Mabuza, Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Health of Eswatini
a444.speech: Expressed gratitude on behalf of the Ministry and the Government of Eswatini, noting that the vehicles would greatly enhance the efficiency of health interventions: "This generous contribution will make a tangible difference in our ability to deliver quality services to the people of Eswatini." ; "Reliable transportation is critical for timely outreach, monitoring, and delivery of health programmes. We are thankful to the United States Government and PEPFAR for their unwavering support."

a444.speaker: Nsindiso Tsabedze, Ministry of Health Communication Officer
a444.speech: Pointed out in an interview with this publication that the vehicles had previously been utilised by other NGOs and hence, the fact that they completed their designed programs, the US saw the Ministry's need and handed over these vehicles.

a458.speaker: BBC Africa Eye investigation
a458.speech: Has revealed how women, known as “madams”, have involved children as young as 13 in prostitution in Kenya; secret filming reveals two different women who say they know it is illegal and then introduce the investigators to underage girls in the sex industry.

a458.speaker: Kenyan police
a458.speech: Said the women and young girls filmed could not be traced; to date there have been no arrests.

a458.speaker: Nyambura, a “madam” in Maai Mahiu
a458.speech: Laughing, says: “They’re still children, so it’s easy to manipulate them by just handing them sweets” ; “Prostitution is a cash crop in Maai Mahiu; the truckers basically fuel it. And that’s how we benefit. It’s been normalised in Maai Mahiu,” she explained, adding that she had one girl as young as 13, who had already been “working” for six months ; “It becomes very risky when you’re dealing with minors. You can’t just bring them out openly in town. I only sneak them out at night in great secrecy” ; when asked whether the clients wear condoms, said she usually made sure they had protection but the odd one did not: “Some children want to earn more [so don’t use them]. Some are forced [not to use them].”

a458.speaker: One of the girls in the house Nyambura led the investigator to
a458.speech: Described being repeatedly abused for sex, on a daily basis: “Sometimes you have sex with multiple people. The clients force you to do unimaginable things.”

a458.speaker: US State Department Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Kenya, 2012 (cited)
a458.speech: Cited an estimate of 30,000 children forced to work in Kenya’s sex industry, a figure derived from the Kenyan government and the now defunct NGO Eradicate Child Prostitution in Kenya.

a458.speaker: 2022 report for the NGO Global Fund to End Modern Slavery (cited)
a458.speech: Found almost 2,500 children were forced into sex work in Kilifi and Kwale counties.

a458.speaker: Cheptoo, a “madam” in Maai Mahiu
a458.speech: Said selling young girls meant she could “earn a living and be comfortable” ; “You carry out this kind of business in great secrecy because it is illegal” ; “If anyone says they want a young girl, I ask them to pay me. We also have our regulars who always come back for them” ; opened up about the profit she makes from them, saying for every 3,000 Kenyan shillings ($23; £17) the girls deliver, her share was 2,500 shillings ($19; £14).

a458.speaker: Underage girl left alone with the undercover investigator by Cheptoo
a458.speech: Told her she had, on average, sex with five men a day; asked what happened if she refused to have sex without a condom, she said she had no choice: “I have to [have sex without a condom]. I will be chased away, and I have nowhere to run to. I am an orphan.”

a458.speaker: Michelle, young woman forced into sex work as a child
a458.speech: Described how, at 12 years old, she lost her parents to HIV and was evicted on to the streets where she met a man who gave her somewhere to live and began sexually abusing her: “I literally had to pay him in kind for educating me. I reached my limit, but I had no-one.”

a458.speaker: Lilian, 19, young woman forced into sex work as a child
a458.speech: Recounted that she lost her parents at a very young age and was left with an uncle who filmed her in the shower and sold the images to his friends, and that the voyeurism soon turned into rape: “That was my worst day. I was 12 then” ; “I am not afraid any more, because Baby Girl is there for me. She is helping us bury the past.”

a458.speaker: “Baby Girl”, 61-year-old former sex worker who provides refuge in Maai Mahiu for girls who have escaped sexual abuse
a458.speech: Told the BBC World Service that, with US President Donald Trump’s decision to pull USAID funding, her outreach programmes – supported by the US aid agency USAID – are about to stop: “From September we will be unemployed,” adding how worried she was about the young women and girls who depend on her: “You see how vulnerable these children are. How would they survive on their own? They are still healing.”

a458.speaker: US government
a458.speech: Did not respond to comments in this investigation about the likely impact of its funding cuts. USAID officially closed last month.

a554.speaker: Danielle Kouassi, director of sustainable cocoa at Olam Food Ingredients (OFI) Côte d'Ivoire
a554.speech: Said the ceremony marks a decisive step in the implementation of the project: "The beneficiaries, now better equipped, will be able to become actors of sustainable development in their respective regions, while contributing to the protection of local ecosystems."

a554.speaker: Jean César Boa, representative of the LMB communities of Indénié-Djuablin
a554.speech: Welcomed the initiative, underlining its impact on the quality of life of the beneficiaries: "We are very happy, because these kits will allow some of our relatives to set up income-generating activities, which will improve their living conditions."

a577.speaker: Agricultural Markets Development Trust (AMDT)
a577.speech: Has called for collective efforts among stakeholders to boost the agriculture sector and contribute fully to the country’s economic growth; said that given the significance of the agricultural sector, there is a need to increase collaborative efforts in various areas, including investing in irrigation farming and the use of quality seeds, to ensure agriculture remains the backbone of the economy.

a577.speaker: Charles Ogutu, AMDT Chief Executive Officer
a577.speech: Said with concerted efforts among stakeholders, the agriculture sector will be able to record higher performance and support the country’s economic development ; “The prosperity of agricultural sector needs collective efforts among stakeholders… Irrigation agriculture will help transform the sector.”

a577.speaker: Delta Shila, Monitoring Result Measurement Officer for AMDT
a577.speech: Said despite promoting the use of quality seeds to the farmers, the institute has been encouraging farmers to engage in irrigation farming to address climate change challenges ; “So far, AMDT has successfully drilled a well worth more than 40m/- in Seluka village, located in Mpwapwa District about 100 kilometers from Dodoma Town” ; noted that AMDT, in collaboration with stakeholders, has already installed solar infrastructure to supply water to the farms, and added that the investment made in the village is part of the implementation of the VACS project, which focuses on promoting cowpea seeds.

a577.speaker: Upendo Makupa, farmer from Seluka Village
a577.speech: Said that the construction of the well has not only aided irrigation farming but also improved access to drinking water in the village; unveiled that before the well was drilled, they had to walk three hours to find water ; “We used to wash our hands only during meals, but after finishing it, we couldn’t wash our hands because water was insufficient.”

a577.speaker: Oziniel Benego, member of the Mkoka Village irrigation group
a577.speech: Said AMDT through its partner – the Agricultural Development Denmark Asia (ADDA) – has enabled them to adopt drip irrigation systems and increase production ; “Previously, we could farm one to five acres due to water scarcity, but after AMDT drilled another well last year, we are now able to farm 25 acres, producing sunflower seeds. This year, after AMDT drilled another well and installed solar infrastructure, we have farmed 41 acres” ; “Before the training and installation of new water infrastructure, farmers were harvesting 2 to 3 sacks of sunflower seeds, but now we are harvesting 5 to 8 sacks per acre.”

a938.speaker: President John Dramani Mahama of Ghana
a938.speech: Has named Shamima Muslim as the new Deputy Presidential Spokesperson, tasking her to work closely with the Acting Presidential Spokesperson, Felix Kwakye Ofosu.

a938.speaker: Shamima Muslim, Deputy Presidential Spokesperson of Ghana
a938.speech: Speaking about her transition from media to politics, shared that her decision was deeply personal and driven by the need to increase women's participation in Ghanaian politics: “The decision to go into politics was not forced on me. There are a lot of people who support political parties behind the scenes, but I wasn't going to use a media platform to execute the political agenda of any political party” ; “I am glad that I was able to do a very professional job that people today can say that yes, you did execute your job professionally guided by the ethics of the profession.”

a987.speaker: Agbeshie, Ghanaian artiste
a987.speech: Said that even though the Volta Region had been overlooked in the past, it has now created its own superstars and developed a thriving music scene: “I can boldly tell you that, over time, the Volta Region has been isolated, or has been left aside in the way. Over the years, the region has created their own superstars, trust me. You see, I’m here today. Anytime I come here to promote them.” ; Noted that because most big artistes are oblivious of the vibrancy of the music market in the Volta Region, they do not consider them in their promotional plans: “The last time I checked, I went to Takoradi to promote my songs. Because I believe there are Ewe’s or whatever are there. So now the artistes that are, excuse me, A-list or big artistes here don’t go to the Volta Region to do anything. So the masses are like, look, if you guys are not coming, no problem, we have our superstars here, we are gonna grow them, and they’ve grown them with time.” ; “So, like, you know, the conversation in North, you can’t go to North without Fancy Gadam and co. Our region has gone to that point where, even, excuse me, no matter how big you think you are here, when you come to Volta Region, they no dey look you, but they’re waiting for Agbeshie because Agbeshie has been in their eyes and their minds over time.”

a1065.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (new report)
a1065.speech: A new report by the International Organization for Migration highlights the worrying situation of 1,024 unaccompanied migrant minors living in Morocco, more than 60% of whom come from other African countries. According to the report, 93% of the minors are aged between 13 and 17, but more than 7% are under 13, an age at which vulnerability is judged critical.

a1065.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (report)
a1065.speech: The report also indicates that 2,196 migrants of 32 different nationalities were voluntarily repatriated to their countries of origin, including 523 to Cote d'Ivoire, 453 to Senegal and 410 to Guinea; that 2,550 Moroccans in an irregular situation abroad, notably in Turkey, benefited from assisted return programmes; and that in terms of resettlement the IOM facilitated the departure of 176 refugees to the United States and 205 to Canada.

a1065.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a1065.speech: On the anti-trafficking front, the IOM reports that 40 victims were assisted, including 10 Moroccans who had been exploited in Oman, Turkey and Thailand, and that twenty-seven foreign victims chose to remain in Morocco, receiving emergency support.

a1065.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a1065.speech: Finally, the organisation notes a clear intensification of social integration efforts: cultural and sporting activities saw their reach multiplied by 200 in 2024, confirming a more inclusive reception strategy.

a1319.speaker: Council of Ministers of Burkina Faso, chaired by Captain Ibrahim Traoré, President of Faso (official communiqué)
a1319.speech: Reported that the Council deliberated on the items on its agenda, heard oral communications, made appointments and authorised missions abroad; that it adopted a report on the 2024 specific projects of the National Bureau of Major Projects of Burkina (BN-GPB) totalling 60,824,529,234 CFA francs financed by the State budget; that it adopted decrees on the collection of revenue for certain services of the General Secretariat of the Government, on declaring SONABEL electricity projects to be of urgent public utility, on approving the statutes of the rail company "FASO RAILS", on mining taxes and royalties, and on the conditions for transferring the State's mining assets; and that it examined and agreed to transmit to the Transitional Legislative Assembly a draft law amending the 1997 law on the coat of arms so as to retain "The Homeland or Death, We Shall Overcome" as the country's motto.

a1319.speaker: Minister of Economy and Finance, acting Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation and Burkinabè Abroad
a1319.speech: Reported to the Council on Burkina Faso's participation in the ministerial conference of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum, held from 09 to 10 November 2024 in Sochi, Russia, which was attended by nearly fifty African countries and was marked by exchanges between the Russian Foreign Minister and the heads of delegation as well as by plenary work.

a1319.speaker: Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation
a1319.speech: Advocated for a multipolar world order free of neocolonialism, in which Africa must play a leading role commensurate with its potential.

a1319.speaker: Participants of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum ministerial conference (joint declaration)
a1319.speech: Adopted a joint declaration on strengthening the various areas of cooperation - the economy, humanitarian affairs, investment, security, the fight against terrorism, culture and education - accompanied by a roadmap for the period 2024-2026.

a1319.speaker: Minister of Humanitarian Action and National Solidarity
a1319.speech: Presented to the Council an assessment of the multisectoral needs of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) who have returned to their localities of origin in five regions of Burkina Faso (Boucle du Mouhoun, Cascades, Hauts-Bassins, Nord and Sud-Ouest), aimed at targeting and adapting multisectoral actions on infrastructure rehabilitation, access to basic social services and restoration of livelihoods; a survey was carried out among 469,898 returned IDPs from 59,972 households in these five regions, and the assessment made it possible to identify the actions to be implemented for their sustainable reintegration.

a1592.speaker: United States (announcement)
a1592.speech: The United States announced the granting of additional aid of more than 22 million dollars to strengthen the resilience and food security of the most vulnerable populations in Madagascar.

a1592.speaker: USAID (statement)
a1592.speech: "This assistance, which will be implemented by consortia led by USAID's partners, Catholic Relief Services and Cultivating New Frontiers in Agriculture, will help marginalised households build sustainable livelihoods, develop their financial capital, and increase their savings and assets," USAID said in a statement.

a1710.speaker: Colonel Boubacar Soumana Garanke, Delegated Administrator of the City of Niamey
a1710.speech: Spoke first to express his satisfaction at celebrating World Humanitarian Day in Niamey. He highlighted the importance of this event in recognizing the efforts of humanitarians in the face of Niger's challenges, notably climate change, security, and access to basic services. He stressed the need for solidarity and international cooperation, while paying tribute to humanitarians for their dedication. He concluded by calling for a collective commitment to strengthen the country's resilience and improve the lives of the most vulnerable.

a1710.speaker: Aissa Laouan Wandarama, Nigerien Minister of Humanitarian Action and Disaster Management
a1710.speech: Expressing deep gratitude on behalf of the President of the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, General Abdourahmane Tiani, and of the Prime Minister, Mr. Mahamane Lamine Zeine, she underlined the importance of the humanitarian community: "Today, we gather to honor this symbolic day. It is essential to understand what the humanitarian community really is. It is a group of people and organizations, local and international, dedicated to emergency assistance for populations in crisis. Their mission is to respond to essential needs while respecting the principles of humanity, neutrality, impartiality, and independence." ; She paid tribute to humanitarian workers and to local communities, the first to intervene in times of crisis, and recalled that the day commemorates the attack on the United Nations House in Baghdad: "This day reminds us that humanity faces an existential threat because of violence in conflicts."

a1710.speaker: Aissa Laouan Wandarama, Nigerien Minister of Humanitarian Action and Disaster Management
a1710.speech: Detailed the impacts of the recent floods, with 281,199 people affected, 105 deaths by drowning, 86 from house collapses, 186 injured, and the loss of 16,766 head of livestock: "We call for increased cooperation with state structures and thank our humanitarian partners for their continued support," she added, stressing that significant efforts are needed to meet growing needs.

a1710.speaker: Harouna Zakou, Country Director of Pathfinder International Niger
a1710.speech: "I am honored to join the great humanitarian family in paying tribute to those who fight every day to improve the lives of Nigerien communities alongside the national authorities." ; "We pay tribute to all humanitarian and development actors who brave difficulties, including insecurity risks and the challenges linked to the rainy season. Despite the floods and cut-off roads, these actors continue to provide health services, economic support, and essential aid to people in distress. Bravo to them for their determination and commitment." ; "For more than 10 years, Pathfinder has worked alongside the Nigerien government to provide access to primary health care, including maternal, neonatal, and child health services, as well as family planning. We are also committed to strengthening the health and economic resilience of women and young people in Niger in the face of daily challenges." ; "I would like to salute and congratulate all Pathfinders for their commitment to providing essential health services to the most deprived populations, despite the obstacles." ; "On this day of celebration, we reaffirm our determination to continue supporting Niger in strengthening the resilience of women, young people, and vulnerable populations."

a1710.speaker: Elh Ahmidou Alhousseini, representative of the NGOs and of SONAH
a1710.speech: Said in his address that he was immensely pleased to join the celebrations, underlining the importance of solidarity and collective action to support families in emergency situations. He called for better protection of civilian populations and paid tribute to the efforts of national and international NGOs to improve conditions for Nigerien communities. His speech reaffirmed the essential role of humanitarian organizations in supporting vulnerable populations and encouraged every citizen to support humanitarian action.

a1710.speaker: Ba Cheick, representative of ECHO
a1710.speech: Recalled the sacrifice of humanitarian workers during the 2003 Baghdad attack. He underlined the courage and altruism of humanitarians in the face of growing humanitarian crises. He highlighted the alarming situation in Niger in 2024, with more than four million people in need of humanitarian assistance, and called for increased support to improve coordination between humanitarian aid and development actions, stressing the importance of strengthening international solidarity to face growing humanitarian challenges.

a1710.speaker: Emmanuel Gignac, interim Humanitarian Coordinator for Niger
a1710.speech: Began by recalling the historic importance of 19 August, marking the tragic 2003 Baghdad attack. He addressed the current humanitarian challenges in Niger, exacerbated by armed violence, the impacts of climate change, floods, and the food crisis. He praised the efforts of the Nigerien government and the security forces, while calling for strengthened international support and durable solutions to meet the urgent needs of Nigerien populations. His speech reiterated the importance of creating conditions for better protection for civilians and humanitarians and of promoting the empowerment of communities so they can break out of the vicious circle of assistance.

a1736.speaker: Study published in Nature Climate Change
a1736.speech: Found that the number of marine heatwave days during the summers of 2023 and 2024 was 3.5 times higher than in previous years, an intensification attributed to climate change and exacerbated by El Nino that caused billions of dollars of damage worldwide ; found that about 10% of the oceans reached record temperatures in 2023-2024, with disastrous impacts on coral reefs, fisheries and coastal communities.

a1736.speaker: The researchers (authors of the Nature Climate Change study)
a1736.speech: Warn that without rapid action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, these marine heatwaves will continue to intensify.

a1736.speaker: Kathryn E. Smith, Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom
a1736.speech: "The number of marine heatwave impacts we have seen over the past two years is quite crazy, with mass coral bleaching, species appearing in new places and the number of related extreme weather events on land." ; "The more regularly our marine ecosystems are hit by marine heatwaves, the harder it is for them to recover from each event."

a1736.speaker: Kathryn E. Smith, Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom
a1736.speech: Warns that adaptation strategies remain limited and do not address the root causes of the phenomenon: "Ultimately, to prevent marine heatwaves and their impacts from getting worse, we must reduce or stop our use of fossil fuels."

a1736.speaker: Earlier research (prior studies cited)
a1736.speech: Has shown that human-caused climate change had already caused a 50% increase in marine heatwaves between 2011 and 2021, and that if no action is taken these phenomena could become 20 to 50 times more frequent and ten times more intense by the end of the century.

a1736.speaker: Professor Thomas Wernberg
a1736.speech: "The heat we are adding to the ocean today will be felt for decades. Without urgent climate action, we are on track to lose important coastal ecosystems, notably kelp forests and coral reefs, within our lifetimes."

a2129.speaker: Mluleki Dlamini, Director of SMEs (Eswatini)
a2129.speech: Announced during the recent National Agriculture and Business Forum that the Government has unlocked E334 million in funding for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, and emphasised that the country's agro-based economy required a shift in strategy to ensure that agriculture becomes a key driver of business growth. ; "The opportunities are there, but we need to change the narrative. Agriculture must be seen as a business, not just subsistence. Investment is the key to unlocking growth." ; According to Dlamini, the E334 million pool, if used responsibly, could stimulate thousands of businesses and improve livelihoods across the country.

a2129.speaker: Mluleki Dlamini, Director of SMEs (Eswatini)
a2129.speech: Acknowledged challenges with some schemes, including high default rates under the Small-Scale Enterprise Loan Guarantee Scheme: "We have seen a worrying number of defaults, which weakens the sustainability of these facilities. Entrepreneurs must approach these funds with seriousness, because they are designed to revolve and benefit others too."

a2129.speaker: Mluleki Dlamini, Director of SMEs (Eswatini)
a2129.speech: Noted the need for stronger involvement from private venture capitalists and institutional investors, who could help expand the financing landscape. ; "We want to see more citizen ownership of enterprises, more co-operatives scaling up, and greater participation by youth and women. That is why we are coupling finance with policy support."

a2213.speaker: Michael Biswick Usi, Vice President of Malawi
a2213.speech: Made a compelling case for reimagining global financing systems, urging international partners to move from rhetoric to action and from pledges to tangible support for nations like Malawi; his addresses centred on the message that Malawi and many nations like it are disproportionately affected by global shocks yet continue to be sidelined in global financial structures; called for a radical shift that would see vulnerability to shocks - like climate change and economic instability - used as a basis for access to concessional financing. "It's no longer enough to name the challenges. The time has come to deliver real, practical solutions," Usi declared at a Commonwealth side event.

a2213.speaker: Michael Biswick Usi, Vice President of Malawi
a2213.speech: Urged reforms in the mandates of multilateral development banks, credit rating systems, and fair access to liquidity for developing nations, arguing in plenary sessions for debt relief and restructuring for nations overwhelmed by repayment burdens, highly concessional loans tailored to LDC realities, enhanced representation of developing countries in financial decision-making spaces, and increased transparency in climate financing mechanisms.

a2213.speaker: Michael Biswick Usi, Vice President of Malawi
a2213.speech: At a high-level roundtable co-hosted by the Gates Foundation and DEVEX, called for targeted financing in health and human capital development: "No development will be sustainable if our people are sick and dying young. Human capital is the bedrock of progress." ; cited the long-standing success of Malawi's HIV programmes, backed by the Global Fund, as evidence that smart, targeted investments in health can yield national dividends.

a2213.speaker: Michael Biswick Usi, Vice President of Malawi
a2213.speech: Strongly condemned the endless cycles of "talk-shop" COP meetings that, in his words, leave Malawi "with no real benefit despite bearing the brunt of climate shocks". "Fancy global statements are not always useful. We need to diagnose our problems and act with precision. The people in the Global South need solutions - not slogans," he said ; "The journey from Seville begins now. Not with more meetings - but with bold, local action backed by fair, global finance."

a2213.speaker: EU officials present at the conference
a2213.speech: Said Usi's candour "cut through the diplomatic fog" that usually clouds such forums.

a2213.speaker: EU Commissioner (unnamed)
a2213.speech: Praised Usi for "telling it like it is."

a2213.speaker: Officials from Norway, Iceland and Luxembourg
a2213.speech: In bilateral meetings with the Vice President, gave reaffirmations of support in key sectors including health, education and governance; Luxembourg, which previously channelled aid through the EU, expressed interest in establishing direct cooperation with Malawi.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: "I worked in the Department of Justice for seven years and during that time I had the opportunity of working on matters to make life better for Americans. But I always wanted to find some way to use my skills and talents to help make things better in Ghana. I, however, didn't see a clear path to doing so. When the MCC opportunity came along and I learned more about what the outfit does and how successful it has been in reducing poverty in the countries it works in, I was excited to join the team," she said about her new appointment in an interview with The Mirror.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: "Of course, it is disappointing to see that after so many years, the power rationing is still continuing but I am excited to be able to play a part to make the situation better," she said. ; She recalled the country experienced a lot of power cuts during her time as a volunteer teacher at Achimota School in 1997 and it was a difficult time for many people; she was, however, impressed with how hardworking and disciplined the students were. ; She said family and friends who knew why she was here all had one refrain: "Ooh, have you heard about 'dumsor dumsor?' You have to solve the 'dumsor' for us," she said with laughter. ; "We want to see this work for Ghanaians. Even more than the inconvenience of the lights off, it is still a serious situation for the economy, people's lives, health, and safety, and we want to make it better," she stated.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: She said she enjoyed her time at Yale Law School, where she said the students and professors were highly motivated and she made many wonderful friends. "During my time at Yale, I felt very much grateful for those who had gone before me and paved the way for me to be there as a black woman from Africa. It definitely imbued a sense in us students that you can do whatever you want to do and that you have a responsibility to attack the biggest problems in the world," she noted. ; She said prior to going to Yale, her father gave her a book called "Becoming Gentlemen", about women in law schools and how they fared, and that one of the lessons she took from it was that in law school women were often counting themselves out of things, not speaking in class and doubting themselves; she was therefore grateful to her dad for the book because it helped her in coaching herself to speak up in class.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: According to Maame, she had been blessed with many great opportunities and also blessed with the ability to take advantage of those opportunities. She said when the MCC opportunity presented itself, she was thrilled to take it because of what the corporation did. "The mission is to reduce poverty around the world and that is a huge responsibility but very fulfilling and the team is very talented and committed to helping people of other countries make their lives better." ; Asked about what she had brought on board, she said her legal skill, passion for the work and the desire to see MCC achieve even greater success in countries around the world were her contribution.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: Said because most of her family live in Ghana, she visited a lot as a child, and that her parents had been an incredible support to her and her sister and they mean the world to her. ; According to Maame, she had no secret to success; what had worked for her, she said, was the support of her family, her huge faith which helped her to navigate difficult situations, believing in herself, as well as knowing her heritage and where she came from.

a2288.speaker: Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong, Vice-President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a2288.speech: "When I speak to younger law students I encourage them to believe in themselves and work hard. You need to ask yourself what it is that you enjoy doing. If you do not see anybody out there doing that kind of job, you can still do it because there is only one you and there are certain things that nobody else can do but you and if that is in your heart and mind, then go for it. To make that happen you have to work hard, believe in yourself, make the best of every opportunity and maintain relationships," she advised. ; "There are going to be challenges but you just have to remember that at any given point in time, your circumstances do not define who you are or your future."

a2491.speaker: Fatma Mwassa, Kagera Regional Commissioner
a2491.speech: Has said the region has sufficient food; speaking to the media at her office, said that during 2023/24 the region produced a total of 3.4 million metric tonnes, while food requirement stood at 770,000 metric tonnes: "I am happy to announce that the region has a surplus of 2.6 million metric tonnes of food. However, people should not relax instead increase the production of cash and food crops."

a2491.speaker: Fatma Mwassa, Kagera Regional Commissioner
a2491.speech: Said the celebrations will be staged at the CCM Complex in Bukoba Municipality starting on October 10 and will reach climax on October 16, 2024 where the Minister for Agriculture, Hussein Bashe will be guest of honour; encouraged citizens to visit the pavilion where people will get education on several critical agricultural issues including modern crop husbandry, livestock and fish cage farming.

a2491.speaker: Fatma Mwassa, Kagera Regional Commissioner
a2491.speech: Appealed to Tanzanians to grab the attractive investment opportunities by increasing production of cash and food crops to enable the nation to get raw materials needed in its industrial drive; challenged Kagera residents to exploit economic opportunities due to its strategic location: "This is a big asset to increase our trade relations."

a2871.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Fiscal Monitor report
a2871.speech: Made known in its Fiscal Monitor report released at the World Bank/IMF Spring meetings that heightened uncertainty caused by the new US tariffs will push global public debt above pandemic-era levels to nearly 100 per cent of global GDP by the end of the decade, adding that the situation could be exacerbated as slower growth and trade strain government budgets; said that in a severely adverse scenario global public debt could reach 117 per cent of GDP by 2027, the highest level since World War II, exceeding reference projections by almost 20 percentage points

a2871.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2871.speech: Said major policy shifts underway have heightened global uncertainty, noting that the series of recent tariff announcements by the United States and countermeasures by other countries have increased financial market volatility, weakened growth prospects, and increased risks; added that rising yields in major economies and widening spreads in emerging markets further complicate the fiscal landscape

a2871.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2871.speech: “We project global public debt to increase by 2.8 percentage points this year—more than twice the estimates for 2024—pushing debt levels above 95 per cent of gross domestic product.” ; “This upward trend is likely to continue, with public debt nearing 100 percent of GDP by the end of the decade, surpassing pandemic levels. These numbers are based on the World Economic Outlook reference projections, reflecting tariff announcements made between Feb. 1 and April 4. Amid substantial policy uncertainty and a shifting economic landscape, debt levels could rise even further.”

a2871.speaker: IMF Fiscal Monitor report
a2871.speech: Said risks to the fiscal outlook have further intensified, noting that debt levels may rise even further than the debt-at-risk estimates if revenues and economic output decline more significantly than current forecasts due to increased tariffs and weakened growth prospects, and that escalating geoeconomic uncertainties could heighten debt risks; said tighter and more volatile financial conditions in the United States may have ripple effects on emerging markets and developing economies, leading to higher financing costs and significantly impacting commodity prices

a2871.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2871.speech: “Demands for fiscal support could also rise for those vulnerable to severe disruptions from trade shocks, pushing up spending.” ; “The Fiscal Monitor estimates that a significant rise in geoeconomic uncertainty could lead to a public debt increase of approximately 4.5 percent of GDP in the medium term.” ; “Limited fiscal improvements may further heighten risks from rising interest rates, especially as many countries have substantial financing needs. High interest rates could limit essential spending on social programs and public investments. Additionally, reduced foreign aid, due to shifting priorities among advanced economies, complicates financing for low-income countries.”

a2991.speaker: Government of Niger
a2991.speech: Denounced, on Tuesday 4 February, the headquarters agreement of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), ordering the closure of its offices and the immediate departure of its expatriate staff.

a2991.speaker: Nigerien authorities
a2991.speech: In November 2024, the Nigerien authorities had expressed concerns about the management of humanitarian aid allocated by the European Union to NGOs, including the ICRC. They had in particular denounced the fact that this aid had been allocated "unilaterally" to NGOs, "in disregard of the principles of transparency and good collaboration."

a3016.speaker: Claire Boucher, known as Grimes, musician and mother of one of Elon Musk’s children
a3016.speech: Wrote on X attacking Musk over his failure to help their child ; Says she has been telling Musk to help this child of theirs, who is currently sick, but the father is doing nothing, which is what made her lose her temper.

a3016.speaker: The Standard (news site)
a3016.speech: According to the site, Musk has fathered twelve children.

a3016.speaker: Reports (unspecified)
a3016.speech: Indicate that Musk is a man who does not let a skirt pass him by.

a3128.speaker: Residents of Ha Tšosane
a3128.speech: Residents believe a chemical reaction may have caused the fire. ; According to residents, this is the second major fire at the Ha Tšosane dumpsite in five years — both believed to have been caused by chemical reactions within the waste.

a3128.speaker: Lebona Lephema, Minister of Local Government, Chieftainship, Home Affairs and Police
a3128.speech: Claimed that an angry community member — frustrated after rubbish was blown into her yard — might have started the blaze in protest. ; He assured Parliament that he had deployed fire extinguishers and water tankers to put out the blaze, adding that investigations were underway to find the culprit.

a3128.speaker: Lebona Lephema, Minister of Local Government, Chieftainship, Home Affairs and Police
a3128.speech: Admitted that he had undertaken study tours to Zimbabwe and South Korea to learn about better waste management practices. He said he returned with Geo Pomona Waste Management (PVT) Ltd of Zimbabwe, which conducted a feasibility study and submitted recommendations. However, he said he was dissatisfied with their report and therefore commissioned another feasibility study, using funds initially budgeted for implementation: “I was not happy with their report, therefore I started another study. Implementation does not necessarily mean moving the dumpsite; even financing the report is part of the implementation.” ; He did not disclose how much of the M20 million had been spent to date but insisted the international trips were funded by the United Nations Environmental Progress.

a3128.speaker: Reitumetsi Kobo, Ha Tšosane resident
a3128.speech: “I just came back to collect a few clothes for the kids. It is impossible to live here. The smoke makes it hard to breathe, and the children were coughing uncontrollably.” ; Said there was no way of knowing how the fire began, since dozens of destitute people are seen daily rummaging through the dump for materials to salvage and sell to recycling companies.

a3128.speaker: Reitumetsi Kobo, Ha Tšosane resident
a3128.speech: “We are tired. For years, we have been fighting for this dumpsite to be moved, but our pleas have continued to fall on deaf ears. Before the fire, strong winds blew trash from the site into our yard, scattering waste all over. Then came the fire.”

a3128.speaker: Reitumetsi Kobo, Ha Tšosane resident
a3128.speech: Describes life near the dumpsite as “unbearable” and worries about thieves breaking into her house while she is away, or the fire gutting her house and belongings: “We are scared that in our absence thieves might break in — or worse, that the fire could spread to our homes. Some families have gone to stay with relatives, but what about those who have nowhere else to go?” ; She said her fears about the long-term health consequences for her minor children growing up exposed to garbage daily are even more stressful.

a3128.speaker: Reitumetsi Kobo, Ha Tšosane resident
a3128.speech: Suspects that water from the dumpsite leaks into their yard, contaminating their water sources: “This water carrying harmful substances from the dumpsite seeps through the foundation into my house. I am already struggling with chest problems after several years of inhaling fumes from the dumpsite daily.”

a3128.speaker: Professor Mosotho George, National University of Lesotho (NUL) — study published in Environmental Analytical Chemistry, May 2019
a3128.speech: His findings noted that because dumpsites in Lesotho, including Tšosane, are not built like modern landfills in developed countries, they lack liners or protective barriers to prevent chemicals from leaching into the soil; results revealed that the soil contained phthalates — chemicals from plastics that may harm people and the environment. He warned that if phthalates are already showing up in the soil, they could eventually creep into water sources or farmland, affecting people, crops, and animals. The study also revealed that such chemicals are difficult to contain, with many phthalates breaking down under heat or acidic conditions.

a3128.speaker: Motlatsi Dlankamandla, local community representative
a3128.speech: Told the Lesotho Times that the government’s silence has grown louder: “The fire burned down some electricity poles and now many families are without power — and still, no action has been taken. I reported it, just like I have reported everything else before.” ; He added that even before the fire, the community had been grappling with severe pollution from the dumpsite, with dirty, contaminated water frequently seeping into homes and farmland: “We can no longer grow vegetables in our gardens because our borehole is contaminated. When we test our farm produce for commercial purposes at testing facilities, we find viruses linked to pollution from the dumpsite. To farm and sell vegetables safely, we have to buy water purification machines.”

a3128.speaker: Motlatsi Dlankamandla, local community representative
a3128.speech: Described the impact of the weekend fire as “too extreme to even put into words”, explaining that the thick smoke has invaded homes and schools, particularly affecting children at Tšosane Primary School: “The children are suffering. Their performance is poor because their environment is toxic. Health-wise, the community is already affected. Now with this fire and suffocating smoke, there is no help — no protective measures. It is business as usual while we choke.”

a3128.speaker: Motlatsi Dlankamandla, local community representative
a3128.speech: Said the community has for years called for the relocation of the dumpsite, but their efforts have been ignored: “We went before a Parliamentary committee. Minister of Local Government, Chieftainship, Home Affairs and Police, Lebona Lephema, told us that the government needed M400 million to move the dumpsite to Tšoeneng, but that money was not available. We are aware that a budget had been allocated this financial year, but no action on the ground shows any development regarding the dumpsite.” ; He said MCC reportedly receives M5 million annually to manage the dumpsite, and this year the budget was increased — but conditions have not improved: “We continue to suffer despite the increased funding. We have tried engaging with the MCC and the town clerk, but nothing has come out of it. There is no transparency, and no progress.”

a3128.speaker: Motlatsi Dlankamandla, local community representative
a3128.speech: Found it bizarre that no emergency medical support was provided, yet waste trucks continued dumping at the already burning site; on Monday morning he asked MCC to provide a mobile clinic for smoke-affected residents, but was told they should go to local health centres. For him and the broader Ha Tšosane community, the lack of urgency has become the “worst insult”: “There is no plan, no accountability, and no care for the people who live at Ha Tšosane. Every time we ask for help, we are ignored — and the only thing that changes is the level of our suffering.”

a3128.speaker: ’Makatleho Mosala, Maseru City Council (MCC) spokesperson
a3128.speech: Contacted for comment on Monday, said the council was doing its best to alleviate the situation.

a3128.speaker: Members of Parliament (National Assembly)
a3128.speech: Interrogated Minister Lephema on the progress made in relocating the dumpsite, since his ministry had been allocated funds for the project, and accused him of misdirecting funds, alleging that money was instead used for international travel and redoing a report, rather than implementing recommendations from a Zimbabwean waste management company hired to study the issue; they said his ministry was not treating the crisis with the urgency it deserved.

a3128.speaker: Dr Mahali Phamotse, leader of the United Africans Transformation (UAT)
a3128.speech: Asked Mr Lephema to explain how his ministry had spent the M20 million allocated this financial year for relocating the Ha Tšosane dumpsite and demanded he disclose the cost of the international trips: “From the report submitted to this House by the Portfolio Committee on Law and Public Safety, of which I am a member, implementation was supposed to happen now. The M20 million was for implementation, not anything else. I am now concerned that the ministry is conducting another study using that money and is already identifying companies to relocate the dumpsite. Where does this lead us? This is among the things that derail this country’s progress. How are they still conducting a study while companies are already being identified? As the committee, we believe the money is already being used, but not for its intended purpose.”

a3128.speaker: Tšeliso Moroke, Matala legislator
a3128.speech: Said the main reason the dumpsite has not been moved to Tšoeneng is that Lesotho still lacks a proper landfill: “The plan is to make a landfill in Tšoeneng, not a dumpsite.”

a3233.speaker: Robert Kennedy, President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
a3233.speech: Has denied being anti-vaccine or spreading misinformation about vaccine safety; said reports accusing him of being anti-vaccine were untrue as he was neither "anti-vaccine or anti-industry": "News reports have claimed that I am anti-vaccine or anti-industry. I am neither. I am pro-safety" ; cited a book he wrote in 2014, saying, "The first line of it is, I am not anti-vaccine, and the last line is, I am not anti-vaccine" ; "I believe that vaccines play a critical role in healthcare. All of my kids are vaccinated" ; "I am pro-safety. I worked for years to raise awareness about the mercury and toxic chemicals in fish, but that didn't make me anti-fish" ; pledged to the senators that, as HHS secretary, he would take no action that discourages or makes it harder for people to get vaccinated, and expressed support for the polio and measles vaccines: "I support the measles vaccine. I support the polio vaccine. I will do nothing as HHS Secretary that makes it difficult or discourages people from taking anything."

a3233.speaker: Robert Kennedy, President Donald Trump's nominee to lead HHS
a3233.speech: Made a U-turn on his views on reproductive rights: during his presidential campaign he had repeatedly described himself as "pro-choice," but at the hearing he said he agreed with President Trump that "every abortion is a tragedy"; he vowed to serve the US president and implement his policies: "I agree with him that we cannot be a moral nation if we have 1.2 million abortions a year. I agree with him that the states should control abortion."

a3233.speaker: Robert Kennedy, anti-vaccine campaigner (past statements)
a3233.speech: Has consistently questioned the safety and efficacy of routine vaccines, including those for hepatitis B and influenza; had propagated a debunked claim linking the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to autism; in 2021 referred to the Covid vaccine as "the deadliest vaccine ever made," despite data showing it's overwhelmingly safe; past statements included that no vaccine was safe and effective, that COVID-19 was targeted to attack Caucasians and Black people, and that it was "highly likely" that Lyme disease was a military bioweapon.

a3233.speaker: Democratic senators at the confirmation hearing
a3233.speech: Accused him of embracing and spreading conspiracy theories to dissuade the public from the use of lifesaving medicines; during the hearing, Democrats brought up some of Mr Kennedy's past statements that no vaccine was safe and effective, and questioned some of his previous remarks made without evidence.

a3233.speaker: Michael Bennet, Democratic US Senator
a3233.speech: Described Mr Kennedy as one who spoke passionately but has a record of half-truths and false statements: "It doesn't matter what you come here and say. It's not reflective of what you really believe."

a3233.speaker: Maggie Hassan, Democratic US Senator from New Hampshire
a3233.speech: Responding to him, said, "There is no reason that any of us should believe that you have reversed the anti-vaccine views that you have promoted for 25 years."

a3233.speaker: American Public Health Association (APHA)
a3233.speech: Said it would "absolutely oppose" Mr Kennedy's nomination.

a3233.speaker: Public health experts and stakeholders
a3233.speech: His nomination as US health secretary had raised concern among public health experts and stakeholders, many of whom feared that his leadership could undermine trust in medical science and established health institutions; they were also concerned that his leadership could affect vaccine and drug production.

a3233.speaker: PREMIUM TIMES (earlier report)
a3233.speech: PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that he had propagated a debunked claim linking the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to autism - a theory rooted in flawed research from the 1990s.

a3281.speaker: United States (official statement)
a3281.speech: The United States has a shared interest with Somalia to advance political and economic stability, prevent terrorism, and address humanitarian crises. Our partnership with the Federal Government of Somalia is key to achieving these objectives. ; The United States is also committed to addressing Somalia’s conflict and climate borne humanitarian challenges... That is why the United States, in particular through the U.S. Agency for International Development, has provided over $1.7 billion in humanitarian assistance to Somalia since 2022 to mitigate the impact of droughts and floods. ; The United States will continue to stand side-by-side with Somalia as it works to achieve its potential.

a3281.speaker: Molly Phee, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs
a3281.speech: Reiterated U.S. respect for Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. She also reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to support Somali-led counterterrorism efforts against al-Shabaab, a brutal and predatory al-Qaida affiliate responsible for countless human rights violations that threatens stability throughout the region.

a3281.speaker: Molly Phee, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs
a3281.speech: Expressed support for an AU-led multinational force to succeed ATMIS while Somalia continues to build its security capabilities.

a3281.speaker: Molly Phee, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs
a3281.speech: Encouraged progress on constitutional reform through a transparent and consultative process.

a3386.speaker: Linda Thomas-Greenfield, US Ambassador to the UN
a3386.speech: Says the relationship between Namibia and the US can be diversified through various means beyond the new compound, and sees this partnership expanding: "partnerships to empower women and youth, who are the powerhouse behind Namibia's economic growth. Partnerships to strengthen inclusive democracy, protect the environment, and, of course, our long-standing partnerships on public health."

a3386.speaker: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, International Relations and Cooperation Minister of Namibia
a3386.speech: While expressing gratitude to the US government for excellent bilateral cooperation, pointed out that Namibia is looking forward to the US partnership in its drive towards green transition and leveraging recent oil and gas discoveries, among others; she also highlighted the importance of the two countries in the promotion of global peace: "For us to work together to ensure international peace and security as well as encourage dialogue and negotiations in solving international disputes. All human rights are equally important, interdependent, and mutually enforced. We don't want to see innocent lives being lost as well as random destruction of property as we continue to see in Gaza."

a3401.speaker: Philasande Phakade and Kgotli Mashile, passengers in the R21 bus crash
a3401.speech: Have recalled the moments before the horror bus crash on the R21 in Ekurhuleni happened.

a3401.speaker: Police (South African Police Service)
a3401.speech: Police initially believed the death to be a suicide, but further investigation pointed to murder.

a3401.speaker: Somerset West Magistrate's Court (court record)
a3401.speech: Granted the accused, former Absa iDirect CEO Jacques Pretorius, R5 000 bail on Tuesday, where he appeared on charges of premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.

a3401.speaker: Kelly Zeegers, employer of Racquel "Kelly" Smith
a3401.speech: Testified the camera system, which only stops recording during power outages, did not capture Smith at the house on 19 February 2024.

a3401.speaker: Racquel "Kelly" Smith (plea explanation)
a3401.speech: Claimed to be working at her boss' house until around midday on the day her daughter disappeared.

a3401.speaker: US State Department
a3401.speech: Is working to implement Trump's executive order to resettle Afrikaners in the US; the order cites the South African government's actions, including the Expropriation Act and alleged discrimination against Afrikaners, as justification.

a3401.speaker: Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, South African Minister of Electricity and Energy
a3401.speech: Supports a "pilot project" using battery storage to reduce peak electricity costs for municipalities, aiming to address Eskom's debt crisis.

a3401.speaker: The Warriors (Eastern Province Cricket team)
a3401.speech: Are disputing their disqualification from the 1-Day Cup after being penalised for not meeting player quotas, claiming other teams haven't faced similar consequences.

a3401.speaker: Cricket South Africa (CSA)
a3401.speech: Disqualified the Warriors for fielding only two black African players instead of the required three, resulting in a hefty fine and point deduction.

a3401.speaker: Eastern Province Cricket
a3401.speech: Argues the decision to field a non-compliant team was based on cricketing needs and awaits CSA's decision on how to resolve the dispute.

a3401.speaker: South African court (ruling)
a3401.speech: Ruled that a TV presenter and actress must return her two young daughters to Germany, their country of habitual residence, under the Hague Convention; the court found insufficient evidence to support the mother's claims that Germany was not the children's habitual residence or that returning them would expose them to harm.

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: Announced on 9 April his candidacy for the presidency of the African Union (AU) Commission, the first to have officially declared his intention to replace Moussa Faki Mahamat.

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On his motivation for running for the AU Commission presidency: "I believe that the profile of this post suits experienced career diplomats very well. It is also a pivotal moment for the institution and therefore for the person who will take the head of the commission. The reforms begun in 2016 by President Paul Kagame must be continued, while many other projects, notably those on the 2063 agenda, have not been carried out. That is the case in particular of the 'Silencing the Guns' project decided in 2013 and which has just been extended to 2030. It is an eminently important file for the stability of the continent and therefore a priority for the next president of the commission." ; On declaring early: "Given the challenges and the stakes the continent faces, there is important awareness-raising work to be carried out in the 55 countries. One never takes too much time to establish and explain a project that concerns not one country or one institution, but an entire continent. Carrying such a project, generating the support it needs, requires a great deal of involvement, of actions to be taken with civil society, the diaspora, NGOs. It is a long-haul task that it is therefore better to begin as early as possible." ; On why to vote for him: "Because we are entering a new phase during which the generation I represent must carry the torch. Diplomatic experience and a good knowledge of the continent's affairs are obviously essential for such a post which, in my view, must go to a convinced defender of multilateralism. For all these reasons, I consider myself ready today to hold such a function."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the AU designation process: "The AU has not yet opened candidate registration. A commission of experts will be set up and it will set a date for the official filing of each candidacy. The list may indeed be longer than was thought at the outset, but it is good news for the continent to have so many competent people available for such an important post. The only thing settled today is that the next president will come from one of the countries of East Africa. It will then be up to the member states to make their choice on the day of the vote."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On relations with Somaliland/Hargeisa: "We have always adopted an attitude of good neighbourliness. We have experienced difficulties in our relations, but our position has always remained the same regarding the territorial integrity of Somalia and we have never deviated one iota from our position."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the Ethiopia-Somalia crisis: "Absolutely. And the fact that we hold the presidency of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) obliges us to assume responsibility for stability in the region. President Guelleh has deployed major efforts, in collaboration notably with Kenya, to avoid a conflict between Ethiopia and Somalia. A great deal of work has been done since February. Delegations from both countries have met on various occasions in Nairobi and we intend to organise a further meeting in Djibouti to, I hope, confirm the de-escalation under way between the two countries."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On Abiy Ahmed's remarks about maritime access: "In this affair, international law must prevail. There is a United Nations convention on the sea which guarantees landlocked countries an outlet to the sea. The Somali president said nothing different: in recognising Ethiopia's rights, he only insisted that this be done within legal, legitimate and recognised frameworks. Our position is identical and that is why we are pushing these countries to reach agreement, but always on the basis of international law, to avoid entering into needless tensions."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On Djibouti's economic relationship with Ethiopia: "For two decades, our mindset has always been to move towards deep integration with Ethiopia. Our two countries are today interconnected in electricity, water, fibre optics... We have a railway line linking our two capitals. Our ports handle nearly 90% of Ethiopian trade and we work enormously to ensure the fluidity of commercial traffic which today is subject to no customs tariff. And it is in Djibouti's interest to continue such cooperation. As our main economic partner, Ethiopia accounts for nearly 50% of our GDP and I think I can say that if Addis Ababa was able to record double-digit economic growth for many years, it is thanks to Djibouti. Abiy Ahmed knows it."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the Sudan crisis and the Paris conference: "It was urgently necessary to mobilise around Sudan. The other crises around the world have diverted attention from this conflict, which remains the deadliest on the continent, but also the most forgotten when it comes to talking about refugees and population displacement. More than 6.5 million Sudanese have had to leave their homes, more than a third of them abroad. The country is sinking into total anarchy without world opinion knowing anything about it. We are witnessing, for example, a proliferation of militias, with an 'ethnicisation' of the conflict that is military at base but is becoming more and more sectarian. We are therefore heading towards the worst-case scenario and it was time for the international community to become aware of it. Two billion euros were announced at the end of the conference to strengthen humanitarian aid and I now hope that a ceasefire can rapidly be decided so that a humanitarian corridor can quickly be opened. Now there is still the question of coordinating the different initiatives. Since this file is first and foremost African, it is essential in my eyes that the platform constituted by IGAD and the AU centralise these different initiatives, wherever they come from. We must not let the Sudanese file become internationalised, otherwise we risk a dilution of results. We therefore defend the simple principle that an African solution must be found to an African problem."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the impact of the Houthi attacks: "Very badly, since it impacts our economy very hard, an economy that depends essentially on maritime trade. Trade is declining, so it disrupts our ports' activities while reducing our supplies, notably from Europe, such as medicines. All this causes additional costs and longer delivery times. Contrary to what some may claim, Djibouti has no reason to rejoice at the situation and we do not applaud the Houthi attacks."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the foreign military bases in Djibouti: "Our foreign policy in matters of defence and security has always been transparent and we have always demanded that Djiboutian soil not be used to carry out offensives against neighbouring countries. Our position is very clear, even with the Americans, who have enough aircraft carriers and bases in the vicinity not to have to use Djibouti for this type of operation. The same goes for our European partners. We agreed to host their ships sent as part of Operation Aspides so that they could escort their vessels and therefore protect their interests. That's all."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the Israeli-Palestinian conflict: "The one we have always held. For forty years, Djibouti has defended the principle of a two-state solution, Israel and Palestine, the only one capable of putting an end to this bloody conflict. There is no other alternative. The security of Israelis is intimately linked to that of Palestinians, so that all can live side by side and in peace. And I believe that world opinion has understood this today."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the renewal of the defence agreements with France: "We are still within the deadlines since the old treaty ends on 1 May. Discussions have been under way for six months and several meetings have been held in Paris and Djibouti. Technical committees have also been set up. We prefer to take the time to be vigilant because this treaty commits us over the long term and we do not want to have to backtrack after six months. The file itself is practically wrapped up. We have made our last amendments and the ball is now in the French court. I think I can say that this treaty will be finalised very soon, because we want to make our partnership with France last." ; On anti-French sentiment across the continent: "Our realities are different. The contexts are not the same in Djibouti and in West Africa. Nor are the states of mind."

a3638.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti
a3638.speech: On the Chinese base in Djibouti: "There is a lot of speculation around this base. What we know is that the Chinese are discreet. Like the others, they escort their merchant ships and protect their interests in the region. I note that after ten years of partnership, Beijing has never had an aggressive policy in the region." ; On the Chinese-American cohabitation in Djibouti: "We are in the middle. So we make sure the fight does not break out at our place. I personally see to it as head of diplomacy."

a3638.speaker: Documentary recently broadcast in France
a3638.speech: According to it, the Chinese base installed in Djibouti could host 10,000 soldiers and its jetty would be sized to receive an aircraft carrier.

a3744.speaker: Aimé Agnanmey, President of the Advisory Council of MCA-Benin
a3744.speech: Welcomed the major advances noted a few months from the end of the programme and considers that MCA-Benin is having an impact on the development of Benin: “The MCA-Benin programme, through its various actions on the ground, is having an impact on the economic and social development of our country, thanks to all of you present here” ; said MCA-Benin owes its success today to all its actors, citing the President of the Republic, Dr Boni Yayi, and the members of the Board of Directors, the Advisory Council and the National Coordination ; “This far from easy task, you had managed to accomplish it up to now with passion and skill. As proof, I cite the handling and use of all the recommendations that we formulate and that are endorsed by the Board of Directors” ; underlined that there will be challenges, but the time to face them will be lacking if actions do not acquire a certain diligence.

a3744.speaker: Samuel Batcho, interim National Coordinator of MCA-Benin
a3744.speech: “The present session is being held practically 15 months from the end of the Grant Agreement, and the challenges to be met are still pressing despite the notable advances recorded in the execution of the various activities of the programme” ; presented the latest advances for each project — the terms of reference for the selection of the printer of the White Paper under ‘Access to Land’ have been drawn up and the resulting draft land code transmitted to the Government; under ‘Access to Justice’ the decree on the One-Stop Shop for Business Formalisation (GUFE) has been adopted and signed and the inter-ministerial order is being signed; under ‘Access to Markets’ the final versions of the feasibility study and tender documents for the Compulsory Control Base (BOC) of the Cotonou industrial fishing port have been submitted and works on lots 1, 2 and 3 continue at the Port of Cotonou; and under ‘Access to Financial Services’ two additional consultants have been recruited to draw up terms of reference and technical specifications.

a3803.speaker: Professor Benyam Dawit Mezmur, deputy dean of postgraduate studies and head of the Children's Rights Project at the University of the Western Cape (UWC)
a3803.speech: Urged participants to confront the deep inequities and blind spots in climate action and to imagine a continent "fit for children" ; "I can confidently say the children's rights space is served better with more politicians and parliamentarians getting involved." ; hailed the seminar's diverse participation and said what united the delegates was "the love we have for the continent of Africa" and a shared ambition "to create an Africa that is fit for children; safer than the one we were handed by our parents."

a3803.speaker: Professor Benyam Dawit Mezmur, deputy dean of postgraduate studies and head of the Children's Rights Project at the University of the Western Cape (UWC)
a3803.speech: Citing a recent article co-authored by Kenyan president William Ruto, said: "A few months ago, president [William] Ruto co-wrote an opinion piece for The Guardian. It said in part, 'Among the many shocks currently facing the international development community is the new direction of the US administration on climate and the implications worldwide for mitigation and adaptation efforts... This is not uncharted territory. While a withdrawal from the Paris climate agreement is undoubtedly a setback, it no longer carries the same level of disruption as it did. The global community has become more resilient and will continue to advance climate action.' I hope this is true for the entire world and for the continent, and I hope it is for the SADC region."

a3803.speaker: William Ruto, President of Kenya (opinion piece co-authored in The Guardian)
a3803.speech: "Among the many shocks currently facing the international development community is the new direction of the US administration on climate and the implications worldwide for mitigation and adaptation efforts... This is not uncharted territory. While a withdrawal from the Paris climate agreement is undoubtedly a setback, it no longer carries the same level of disruption as it did. The global community has become more resilient and will continue to advance climate action." ; in that article, warned that international development efforts are increasingly being shaped and, in some cases, jeopardised by shifting US foreign policy priorities, particularly in the wake of dramatic aid cuts and retreat from multilateralism.
